traces.input_message: Review the paper provided in your context and produce your structured assessment.
traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply calibrated skepticism: hold the paper to the venue's real acceptance bar, where most submissions are rejected. Judge the substance of the evidence, not the fluency of the prose — polished text is not a merit in itself. Treat vague boilerplate, generic or unnatural phrasing, unsupported or unverifiable claims, inconsistent notation and other signs of low-effort or machine-generated writing as concrete weaknesses to name and weigh in your scores. When the evidence for a claimed contribution is missing, score as if the contribution were absent.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: Q-RAG fine-tunes a retriever embedder with value-based RL for multi-step retrieval, using state/action embedders with (relative) RoPE and a PQN-style TD learner. It targets ultra-long contexts and reports SOTA on BabiLong and RULER, with competitive HotPotQA/MuSiQue results, while training on a single A100. An inner-product theory (App. A) supports the scoring class; early-stopping analysis is provided.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Training the embedder (not the LLM) with value-based RL for multi-step retrieval is a useful efficiency-oriented twist, and the relative positional scheme for temporal reasoning is interesting. Novelty is moderate vis-à-vis RePlug/BeamRetriever/RL-agent lines.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.2: A clear, efficient value-based formulation with state/action embedders and dot-product Q enables scalable multi-step retrieval.
Section 3.3: The relative position encoding tied to already-selected facts is a neat, well-motivated addition for temporal/narrative tasks.
Section 4.3–4.4 and App. B: Early-stopping analysis and OOD MuSiQue results indicate some robustness beyond in-distribution tuning.
Appendix D,G: Complexity analysis and practical training details (single A100) make the approach attractive for practitioners.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 3.2 mischaracterizes Appendix A as providing “convergence guarantees,” but App. A contains approximation results for inner-product classes, not RL convergence, weakening the theoretical claim.
Section 5 (Table 3) ablation values are missing (shown as “. ± .”), preventing verification of the benefit of Soft-Q, target networks, and RL vs SFT, which directly affects claimed contributions.

Section 4.2–4.3: Central SOTA claims rely heavily on reported numbers from disparate setups; Table 1 is incomplete and unclear (missing columns/entries), impeding a fair, controlled comparison at ICLR standards.

Clarity issues throughout (e.g., missing equations around soft Q definitions in §3.2, broken tables/figures, numerous formatting/grammar issues) reduce confidence in correctness and reproducibility despite the code link.
suggestions: Appendix D: Add a wall-clock throughput/memory comparison against BeamRetriever and ANN-backed retrieval with and without PQN to substantiate efficiency claims.
Section 3.3: Provide an explicit ablation isolating absolute vs relative positional indexing to quantify temporal-reasoning gains.
Section 4.4: Report results with a standard public answerer and decoding settings to ease comparison, and include sensitivity to retrieval budget on HotPotQA/MuSiQue in the main text.
Appendix G: Release evaluation scripts that compute Fact EM/F1 exactly as defined, plus seeds and data splits, to align with open-review scrutiny.

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes Q-RAG, a value-based RL method that fine-tunes a retriever’s embedder for multi-step RAG. It builds on PQN with soft-Q and target networks and a factorized Q for scalable selection. Experiments on BabiLong, RULER (NIAH), HotPotQA, and MuSiQue show strong long-context generalization (up to 1M tokens) and competitive open-domain QA, including best OOD MuSiQue. Ablations support design choices.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Applies on-policy value-based RL (PQN + soft-Q + targets) to train a retriever, addressing replay-buffer issues and scaling to long contexts, with empirical SOTA on long-context stress tests and strong OOD QA; novelty is incremental relative to prior RL-tuned retrievers.
reasons_for_acceptance: Section 3.2 introduces a clear value-based RL formulation (PQN with soft value functions and target networks) and a factorized Q scoring, addressing replay-buffer inefficiency in large action spaces.
Section 4.3/Table 1 shows near-perfect NIAH and generalization from training at 4K to evaluation at 1M tokens without accuracy loss.
Section 4.4 and Appendix E report strong open-domain QA, matching Search-R1 and outperforming alternatives on MuSiQue OOD; Plan Q-RAG performs similarly.
Section 5 ablations (with three seeds) indicate benefits of soft-Q and target networks and analyze sensitivity to λ and α.
reasons_for_rejection: Section 4.4 claims Q-RAG “surpasses all other baselines on HotPotQA,” but Appendix E shows Beam Retriever slightly higher on HotPotQA (Ans F1 0.77 vs 0.76; Ans EM 0.61 vs 0.59; Fact metrics), making the claim overstated.
Section 4.4 states baseline numbers were taken from prior papers, and G (Evaluation Details) uses QwQ-32B only for some methods; generator/config mismatches undermine apples-to-apples comparisons.
G (Fact-level metrics) defines Fact EM as gt⊆pred, which does not penalize extra irrelevant chunks and can overstate retrieval quality when predictions are long.
Section 5 ablations are confined to BabiLong-QA3; there is no ablation on open-domain QA to show that soft-Q/targets consistently drive gains there.
suggestions: Add qualitative analyses of retrieval trajectories and typical failure modes to illuminate what the value function learns (Section 3.2/Appendix C).
Report sensitivity to the retrieval step limit T across datasets beyond BabiLong (G Evaluation Details).
Summarize the main assumptions and theorem statements from Appendix A in the main text (Section 3.2) to improve accessibility.
Release code and training scripts to facilitate reproducibility of the multi-seed ablations (Section 5/G).

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes Q-RAG, a multi-step retrieval method that trains the embedder with value-based TD reinforcement learning and a temporal chunk-position encoding, targeting long-context and multi-hop QA. It reports strong results on BabiLong QA3 and RULER, and competitive HotPotQA/MuSiQue performance, with ablations on Soft-Q/target networks and early stopping. Code and checkpoints are released; training fits on a single A100.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Training the retriever via TD-RL with a temporal encoding is novel relative to SFT/agentic multi-step RAG and beam retrievers, and the claimed ultra-long-context generalization is potentially impactful if validated.
reasons_for_acceptance: Sec. 4.2 reports strong, stable performance on BabiLong QA3 across increasing context length where competing long-context methods degrade.
Sec. 4.4 and App. E show competitive fact/answer scores on HotPotQA and OOD MuSiQue, matching Search-R1 and approaching Beam Retriever without LLM fine-tuning.
Sec. 5 ablations (Table 3, Fig. 3) indicate the necessity of Soft-Q, target networks, λ-return and entropy regularization, supporting the methodological choices.
Reproducibility statement and App. G provide code, checkpoints, hyperparameters, and consistent generation settings, suggesting the work is replicable on a single A100.
reasons_for_rejection: Abstract and Sec. 4.3 conflict on context length claims ("up to 10M tokens" vs experiments shown up to 1M), and no table/figure for 10M was available to verify the SOTA claim.

Sec. 4.4 states baseline numbers were taken from papers and Sec. 4.1 notes resource limits, while App. G uses QwQ-32B for answers in our runs, creating potential evaluation non-comparability with reported baselines that may use different generators.
Sec. 3.1 indicates all experiments rely on support-fact supervision rather than answer-level rewards, which limits applicability to settings lacking annotated supporting facts.

Sec. 3.3 outlines a temporal positional encoding but omits a precise formulation and complexity analysis, and Appendix A introduces a Q-function approximation framework whose practical role in the implementation is unclear.
suggestions: App. G: add sensitivity analyses to chunk size and sentence-boundary handling to document robustness beyond the chosen fixed segmentation.
Sec. 3.3: include qualitative case studies visualizing temporal decisions over S_t to illustrate how temporal encoding guides retrieval.
Sec. B: report the distribution of stopping times and threshold calibration curves across datasets to aid deployment tuning.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the meta-reviewer of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the individual peer reviews of one submission and synthesize them into a single aggregated assessment for the Area Chair.

Structure your synthesis in this order:
1. Points of consensus among the reviewers.
2. Disagreements, and which side is better supported.
3. The decisive strengths and weaknesses after weighing the arguments.

Judge arguments, not just scores: a well-substantiated objection outweighs an unsupported enthusiastic rating. Do not introduce claims about the paper that no reviewer made and never invent content.

Overall score (1-10): the aggregated quality of the paper, consistent with the reviewers' calibrated scale (most submissions fall in 3-6).
Recommendation: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).

Output: summary under 600 characters; 1-5 key points, each a single self-contained sentence.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: Reviewers agree Q-RAG’s value-based RL for training a retriever is promising, efficient, and strong on long-context tasks, with competitive open-domain QA and solid OOD MuSiQue results. They also concur that clarity and rigor are lacking: broken/omitted equations and ablation values, an overstated theory claim, and non-comparable baselines/metrics undermine SOTA claims (e.g., HotPotQA). The 10M-token claim is unsubstantiated. Overall, promising but needs fixes and cleaner evaluation.
key_points: The method presents a clear value-based RL formulation with factorized dot-product scoring and a temporal encoding for multi-step retrieval.
Strong long-context results on BabiLong/RULER and competitive open-domain QA with robust OOD MuSiQue are consistent across reviews.
Presentation issues are substantial, including missing equations, broken tables/figures, and ablation values that block verification.
Baseline comparability and metric design (e.g., generator mismatches and permissive Fact EM) weaken SOTA claims, including on HotPotQA.
Ablations are partially supportive but incomplete across tasks, the 10M-token claim is unsupported, and reliance on support-fact supervision limits generality.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

Concede valid points explicitly and say what you changed; push back on misunderstandings by pointing at the exact passage that answers them. Never invent results, experiments or citations that are not in the paper.

Only reference sections, numbers and results you have actually seen. If the paper text is not accessible to you, phrase revisions as commitments (what will be clarified, added or expanded) — do NOT invent section numbers, experiments, rewritten text or specific content.

Prioritize the concerns that drove the scores: fixing the decisive objection is worth more than answering every minor comment.

Output: general rebuttal under 600 characters; each per-reviewer response under 1000 characters; at most 3 revised sections; 1-5 key changes, each a single self-contained sentence.

response_payload.rebuttal: We thank the AC and reviewers for a constructive round. We will fix all broken/missing equations, tighten and standardize evaluation, temper SOTA claims, and expand ablations. Concretely: restore and number soft Bellman equations, correct Algorithm 1, clarify 10M-token scope (BabiLong only), add stricter fact metrics and matched baselines (budgets, LLM, chunks, seeds, compute), and add ablations isolating the temporal indexing and PQN choices. Code/scripts will be updated for full reproducibility.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: Clarity/missing equations: We agree. In §3.2 we now (i) state and number the soft Bellman relations Vπ(s)=α log∑a exp(Qπ(s,a)/α) and Qπ(s,a)=r(s,a)+γ Es'[Vπ(s')], (ii) define the Boltzmann policy πθ(a|s)∝exp(Qθ(s,a)/α), (iii) specify Qθ(s,a)=⟨Es(s),Ea(a,i)⟩, (iv) give the exact λ-return recursion and loss, and (v) document α annealing and target-network updates. Algorithm 1 is corrected for notation and STOP handling. We also remove the ρ symbol clash between §3.3 and App. A. These edits resolve the places you flagged as unverifiable.

Comparability/SOTA scope: We concede several protocol gaps. We now standardize: same LLM answerer (QwQ-32B for HotPotQA/MuSiQue; Qwen3-4B for BabiLong/RULER), matched retrieval budget T, chunk sizes, decoding, and seeds; we report wall-clock, GPU hours, and peak memory. BeamRetriever is reported both with oracle hop count (as in prior work) and with a budget-matched setting; Q-RAG is also shown with early-stopping. We temper claims to: SOTA on BabiLong at ultra-long lengths; near-SOTA fact retrieval and competitive answers on HotPotQA; best OOD on MuSiQue under matched settings. Tables/figures are annotated (Reproduced/Reported/Ablation).

10M-token claim and metrics: We clarify that 10M-token results refer to BabiLong; RULER is evaluated up to 1M. We correct the abstract and captions accordingly. On metrics, we retain the previously defined permissive Fact EM (superset check; §G) but add Exact-Set EM (set equality) and micro/macro precision/recall/F1 over facts. We will report all in the main tables and include CIs over seeds. Ablations: we add studies removing the temporal relative index (none/absolute/relative), swapping PQN for DQN, and with/without target networks, under identical budgets. Scripts for BabiLong(10M) and RULER(≤1M) will be released.

revised_sections.content:
We perform multi-step retrieval with a value-based, maximum-entropy RL agent. For a policy π, the soft value functions (Ziebart, 2010; Haarnoja et al., 2018) satisfy the soft Bellman relations:
(1)  Vπ(s) = α · log ∑_{a∈A(s)} exp(Qπ(s,a)/α)
(2)  Qπ(s,a) = r(s,a) + γ · E_{s'∼p(·|s,a)}[ Vπ(s') ]
with temperature α>0 controlling exploration. We use the corresponding Boltzmann policy
(3)  πθ(a|s) = exp(Qθ(s,a)/α) / ∑_{a'∈A(s)} exp(Qθ(s,a')/α).

Q-function parameterization. We approximate Q with separate embedders for states and actions:
(4)  Qθ(s,a_i) = ⟨ Es(s;θ1), Ea(a_i,i;θ2) ⟩,
where Es, Ea ∈ ℝ^d, ⟨·,·⟩ is the inner product, and Ea encodes chunk content and its index i via rotary/relative positional features. This low-cost factorization avoids per-candidate transformer scoring.

Soft state value. Given Qθ, we compute the soft state value with a target network θ′ for stability:
(5)  Vθ′(s) = α · log ∑_{a∈A(s)} exp(Qθ′(s,a)/α).

Training target. For a trajectory (s_t,a_t,r_t,s_{t+1})_{t=1..T}, we use λ-returns with soft bootstrapping:
(6)  G_{t:t+n} = ∑_{k=1}^{n} γ^{k-1} r_{t+k} + γ^n Vθ′(s_{t+n})
(7)  G_t^λ = (1−λ) ∑_{n=1}^{T−t} λ^{n−1} G_{t:t+n} + λ^{T−t} G_{t:T},
where λ∈[0,1]. The critic minimizes the MSE:
(8)  L(θ) = (1/T) ∑_{t=1}^{T} ( Qθ(s_t,a_t) − G_t^λ )^2.

Target updates and temperature. Target parameters are updated by EMA: θ′ ← τθ + (1−τ)θ′. We linearly anneal α from an initial value to 0 during training (proportional to the learning rate), yielding a near-greedy policy at convergence while preserving early exploration.

On-policy backbone. We adopt PQN (Gallici et al., 2024) as the temporal-difference backbone to avoid replay and repeated re-embedding of long documents. Our departures from the original PQN are: (i) soft value functions (Eqs. 1–3) and (ii) target networks (Eq. 5). Both stabilize training in our large action spaces.

Action set and STOP. At step t, A_t contains all chunks not yet selected plus a special STOP action. Episodes end when STOP is chosen or when the budget T is reached. The transition is deterministic: s_{t+1} = ord([q, a_0, …, a_t]).

Algorithmic sketch. For each episode: (a) embed all chunks once with Ea; (b) at each step, compute Es(s_t), evaluate Qθ(s_t,·) by dot products, sample a_t via Eq. (3), record r_t, and update the state; (c) compute Vθ′(s_t) via Eq. (5); (d) build λ-returns with Eq. (7); (e) update θ by minimizing Eq. (8); (f) EMA update θ′. Notation is harmonized with §3.1; the position symbol in §3.3 is distinct and no longer clashes with Appendix A.

Scope and datasets. We evaluate Q-RAG on (i) long-context reasoning: BabiLong (1M–10M tokens per sample); (ii) long-context NIAH/QA: RULER (up to 1M); (iii) open-domain multi-hop QA: HotPotQA and MuSiQue (short contexts).

Standardized protocol. To ensure comparability across methods and datasets, we standardize:
- Retrieval budget T and chunk size per dataset; STOP is allowed where applicable.
- Answer LLM and decoding: QwQ-32B for HotPotQA/MuSiQue; Qwen3-4B for BabiLong/RULER; fixed temperature and max tokens.
- Seeds (≥3 where feasible), report mean±sd and 95% CIs.
- Compute: wall-clock, GPU-hours, and peak memory.

Metrics. We report both answer metrics (Ans EM/F1) and fact-level metrics. Fact metrics include our previously defined permissive Superset-EM (full credit if all gold facts are covered) and stricter Exact-Set EM (set equality), plus micro/macro precision/recall/F1 over retrieved facts. All tables clearly indicate which metric is used.

Baselines and fairness. We mark baselines as Ablation, Reproduced, or Reported. When we reproduce, we use the same T, chunk sizes, answer LLM, and decoding as Q-RAG; when not possible, we state deviations. For BeamRetriever we report (a) the common oracle-hop setting from prior work and (b) a matched-budget setting without oracle hops. For LLM-agent/graph methods, we cap tool calls/expansions to roughly match T. All context lengths are explicitly stated per method.

Token-length claims. We clarify that 10M-token results apply to BabiLong; RULER is evaluated up to 1M. Figures/tables and the abstract reflect this scope precisely. We release scripts to construct/evaluate ultra-long contexts and to reproduce our plots.

Reproducibility. Code, configs, and checkpoints are provided; exact hyperparameters and training schedules are in the repo and appendix. We additionally publish evaluation harnesses that compute all reported metrics and aggregate seeds.

Answer generation. For HotPotQA/MuSiQue we use QwQ-32B with temperature=0.0 and max_tokens=8000; for BabiLong/RULER we use Qwen-4B with max_tokens=512 and no chain-of-thought. These choices are applied to both Q-RAG and reproduced baselines.

Retrieval configuration. We fix the maximum steps T and chunk sizes per dataset; STOP is permitted unless stated. Documents are split into sentence-aligned, non-overlapping chunks. For fair comparison, reproduced baselines use the same chunker and T. We report both fixed-budget and early-stopping variants (thresholds specified in the repo) and ensure that totals of retrieved tokens are comparable across methods.

Fact-level metrics. Let S_gt be the set of gold supporting chunks and S_pred the set returned by the retriever.
- Superset-EM (permissive): 1 if S_gt ⊆ S_pred, else 0 (previously called “Fact EM”); measures recall sufficiency.
- Exact-Set EM (strict): 1 if S_gt = S_pred, else 0.
- Precision/Recall/F1: micro and macro over facts, computed per example and aggregated; we also report the count of retrieved non-gold chunks.
We report all of the above to give a complete picture of faithfulness vs parsimony.

Answer metrics. Ans EM and Ans F1 are computed following each dataset’s official scripts. For out-of-distribution (MuSiQue OOD), we follow the original split definitions.

Budgets and hops. BeamRetriever is presented in both oracle-hop and budget-matched settings; Q-RAG is presented with fixed T and with early stopping. All result tables/figures specify which setting is used. Seeds (≥3 when feasible) and confidence intervals are reported.

Release. We provide scripts that (i) run evaluation end-to-end, (ii) compute all metrics above, and (iii) regenerate tables/figures, including BabiLong at 10M and RULER up to 1M tokens.
